Each day started the same. At first, it had been the novelty of a new chapter in a worn book, each morning an opportunity to start anew. But after years of waking to the same routine, the excitement began to fade into numb acceptance. The sun rose each day without fail, and the rituals became the only constants in a life that otherwise ebbed and flowed with the monotony of repetition.

Lena sat on the edge of her bed, her old gray blanket pulled tightly around her shoulders as she observed the remnants of her previous life scattered across the room—empty pill bottles, tattered books, faded photographs. They were reminders of the woman she used to be, with dreams and hopes, before the days blended together into a single, grey expanse.

The door creaked open, and Lena didn't have to look to know who it was. Every day at exactly six in the morning, her neighbor, Mr. Thompson, the elderly widower, would bring her breakfast, their only point of contact in this silent dance of existence. Today was no different; he placed a thermos and an extra slice of toast on her kitchen table before turning and leaving.

With the same mechanical motions, Lena prepared her morning ritual, each gesture a reminder of the unchanging nature of her life. She drank her lukewarm tea, read the news from yesterday's paper, and pondered why anything could ever change.

"Your neighbor, Mrs. Lee," Mr. Thompson said one day, his voice a soft murmur through the closed door. "She seems so… content."

Lena didn't respond, but she could imagine him shaking his head, disappointment etched onto his face. How could she explain the quiet resignation that filled her soul?
